History:
• 45-year-old woman presents with painful, itchy, cracked, very dry skin on the palms for 3–4 months.  
• Onset shortly after starting a new housekeeping job; symptoms progressively worsened and now limit ability to work (missed last 3 days).  
• Location: mainly palms; mild generalized dryness on legs.  
• Associated symptoms: intermittent itch; occasional bleeding only after scratching.  
• Denies fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary changes; appetite intact.  
• Exposures/Triggers: Frequent contact with cleaning chemicals at hotel; often does not wear protective gloves.  
• Previous attempts: OTC E-45 emollient and an unspecified antihistamine—no improvement.

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• Medications: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented); OTC E-45 cream; OTC antihistamine (name/dose not documented).  
• Allergies: No known drug or other allergies.  
• Family history: Diabetes; no known dermatologic, asthma, or bowel disease.  
• Social: Hotel housekeeper; non-smoker; alcohol ≈2 pints beer/week.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-visit—visual exam not documented.  
• Patient reports marked palmar dryness, fissuring/cracking, intermittent itch, occasional bleeding when scratched.  
• No reported swelling, erythematous rash elsewhere, or systemic signs.  
• Other exam elements not recorded.

Impression:
Probable irritant contact dermatitis of the palms (occupational hand dermatitis).  
DDx consistent with transcript:  
1. Irritant contact dermatitis – high likelihood; direct chemical exposure without gloves, pain/fissures > itch.  
2. Allergic contact dermatitis – medium likelihood; same exposure setting, intermittent itch.

Management Plan:
• Education: Strict avoidance of triggers; wear protective gloves at all times during cleaning.  
• Medications prescribed:  
  – Topical steroid cream (potency/type and dosing not documented) for palmar inflammation.  
  – “Stronger” emollient moisturizer to be applied liberally 3–4 times daily for the next 2 weeks.  
• Follow-up: Re-evaluation in 10–14 days if no improvement; sooner if lesion spreads or worsens.  
• Prescription sent electronically to patient’s pharmacy.  
• Advise return earlier if increased pain, bleeding, infection signs, or functional impairment.

Patient Summary:
Ms. Laura Parkinson, 45, presents with 3–4 months of painful, fissured palmar skin likely due to occupational irritant contact dermatitis from unprotected exposure to cleaning products. She will begin topical steroid therapy, intensive moisturization, and consistent glove use, with follow-up arranged in 1–2 weeks.

Key Takeaways:
• Wear gloves whenever using cleaning chemicals.  
• Apply prescribed steroid and emollient to palms 3–4×/day for 2 weeks.  
• Return promptly if no improvement, spreading rash, or worsening pain.

Next Steps:
• Monitor response; revisit in 10–14 days or sooner if deterioration.  
• If inadequate response, consider patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis or referral to dermatology.
